36.title: Through the roof (Mark 2:1–12)
36.hook: four friends dig through a roof to lower their paralyzed friend to Jesus
36.howItsDone: Catholics pray for one another and ask the saints for their prayers, and the Church offers the sacraments of healing, confession and the anointing of the sick, which the Catechism connects with stories like this one.

segments.voice: Last week ended at Cana, where the wine ran out and Mary said, do whatever he tells you. Day thirty-six starts a new week: healings and encounters.
screen: `DO WHATEVER HE TELLS YOU.` → `WEEK SIX: HEALINGS AND ENCOUNTERS.`

segments.voice: Capernaum, a fishing town on the lake. Word gets around that Jesus is back, staying in a house, and the house fills. Then the doorway. Then the street outside. Mark says there was no room, not even at the door. Now four men come down the street carrying a mat, and on the mat is their friend. He can't walk. He can't get himself anywhere. They reach the crowd and stop. There's no way through. It would be easy to turn around. Maybe tomorrow, when it's quieter. These four look up.
screen: `A HOUSE PACKED TO THE DOOR.` → `FOUR MEN CARRYING A MAT.` → `NO WAY THROUGH. THEY LOOK UP.`

segments.voice: So they climb onto the roof, carrying him, and start digging. Mark says they uncovered the roof, broke it open, and let down the mat. Imagine being inside: dust and bits of clay falling on everyone, daylight opening in the ceiling, and a man lowered into the middle of the sermon. Now the line to catch. Mark says: when Jesus saw their faith. The friends'. We don't hear a word from the man on the mat; it's the four who carried him whose trust Jesus sees. Then Jesus says something nobody expected: "Son, thy sins are forgiven thee." Some scribes sitting there are troubled, reasoning in their hearts: who can forgive sins but God alone? Jesus asks them which is easier to say, your sins are forgiven, or get up and walk. Then, so they'll know he has that authority, he turns to the man: "Arise, take up thy bed, and go into thy house." And he does, in front of everyone, carrying the mat that carried him. The crowd says: we never saw the like. The Church hears two things here. One is the sacraments of healing, confession and the anointing of the sick, where forgiveness and healing are asked for together. The other is intercession: carrying someone to God when they can't get there themselves. That's what Catholics are doing when they pray for each other, and when they ask the saints to pray for them.

segments.voice: Think of one person who can't get where they need to be right now, someone sick, or stuck, or too worn out to ask for help, and picture yourself as one of the four at the corners of the mat. If you pray, carry them to God in your own words, or with a prayer you know. If you don't, hold them in mind with care, and ask yourself which corner of the mat you could lift this week.

37.title: The tax collector's table (Matthew 9:9–13)
37.hook: Matthew is called from his booth and throws a dinner full of the wrong people
37.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Matthew, apostle and evangelist, on September 21, when this Gospel is read at Mass; Pope Francis's episcopal motto, miserando atque eligendo, comes from Saint Bede's homily on it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, four friends went through the roof with a man on a mat. Your line: friends dig through roofs.

Think of the least popular job in your town. The person who tows your car. The one who sends the final notice. Now make it worse: this person works for the occupying power, and everyone assumes they skim a little extra for themselves. That was a tax collector in Galilee. In Capernaum there was a toll booth, and in it sat a man named Matthew. People crossed the street to avoid him. Pious people wouldn't eat with him. One day Jesus walks past the booth, stops, looks at him, and says two words.
screen: `THE LEAST POPULAR JOB IN TOWN.` → `MATTHEW AT HIS BOOTH.` → `TWO WORDS.`

segments.voice: The two words: "Follow me." The Gospel that carries his name says simply: "And he arose up and followed him." No speech, no conditions. He gets up from the money and goes. Mark and Luke tell the same story and call him Levi. Then comes the dinner. Jesus sits at table in the house, and many tax collectors and sinners come and eat with him and his disciples. Matthew has invited everyone he knows, and everyone he knows is the wrong crowd. Some Pharisees, who took holiness very seriously, ask the disciples: why does your master eat with tax collectors and sinners? In that world, sharing a table meant sharing a life. Jesus answers with a picture from medicine: "They that are in health need not a physician, but they that are ill." Then he sends them to the prophet Hosea: "I will have mercy and not sacrifice." A doctor who avoids sick people isn't much of a doctor. He came for the ones who know they need help. Catholics keep Matthew's feast on September twenty-first. In Rome, a famous Caravaggio painting catches this moment: a beam of light across a dark counting table, and a man pointing at himself, as if to say, me? And Pope Francis took his motto from an old homily by Saint Bede about this scene. In Latin: miserando atque eligendo. Roughly, by having mercy, and by choosing. He looked at Matthew with mercy, and chose him.

Notice what rises in you: awkwardness, judgment, maybe curiosity. Then picture the look Jesus gave Matthew, and imagine being looked at that way yourself; if you pray, you can ask for that look.

38.title: The woman at the well (John 4:1–42)
38.hook: at noon, alone, a Samaritan woman has the longest conversation with Jesus in the gospels
38.howItsDone: Catholics read this Gospel on the Third Sunday of Lent in Year A, especially with those preparing for baptism at Easter; Eastern Christians honor the woman as Saint Photini.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the publican's table, full of the wrong people. Your line: he came for the sick.

About the sixth hour, John says: around noon, in the heat of the day. A woman comes alone, carrying her jar to Jacob's well outside a Samaritan town. John doesn't say why she came at that hour. Maybe it was nothing. Some readers wonder if it was easier than facing the others. Sitting by the well, tired from the road, is a Jewish man she's never seen. John adds a short note: Jews and Samaritans did not share things with each other. And the man looks up and speaks to her.
screen: `ABOUT THE SIXTH HOUR.` → `ONE WOMAN, ALONE.` → `A STRANGER AT THE WELL.`

segments.voice: He says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Give me to drink." She's startled. How is it that you, a Jew, ask a drink of me, a Samaritan woman? He crossed two lines at once, and she noticed both. Then he turns it around: if you knew who was asking, you'd have asked him, and he'd have given you living water. In Greek, living water also meant running water, fresh from a spring, as against a still cistern. She takes him literally: you have no bucket, and the well is deep. He goes further. Whoever drinks this water will be thirsty again, but the water he gives becomes a spring inside, welling up to eternal life. Then he tells her to call her husband. She says she has none. He tells her she's had five, and the man she has now isn't her husband. The Gospel never says why. Widowhood, divorce, a hard life: John is silent, and he never has Jesus condemn her. She doesn't run. She asks a real question, about where God should be worshiped, this mountain or Jerusalem. He says the hour is coming when true worshipers will worship in spirit and in truth. Then she leaves her water jar and goes back into the town: "Come, and see a man who has told me all things whatsoever I have done." And many believe because of her. In the East she's honored as a saint, called Photini, the enlightened one. Catholics hear her story in Lent, with those preparing for baptism at Easter.

39.title: Only say the word (Matthew 8:5–13)
39.hook: a Roman officer asks healing for his servant and says he isn't worthy to have Jesus under his roof
39.howItsDone: At every Mass, just before Communion, the congregation says together a response adapted from the centurion's words, asking to be healed in soul.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the woman at the well and living water: a long, honest conversation at noon. Your line: he waited at the well.

If you've ever been to a Catholic Mass, you've heard today's story, even if you didn't know it. Just before Communion, the whole church says a line together, a line about a roof. It comes from a Roman soldier: a centurion, an army officer, a foreigner serving the power that rules the land. He's used to giving orders. People step aside when he walks by. And one day in Capernaum he comes up to a Jewish teacher from Nazareth and asks for help. Not for himself. For his servant, lying at home, paralyzed and suffering terribly.
screen: `A LINE SAID BEFORE COMMUNION.` → `A ROMAN OFFICER.` → `HE ASKS FOR HIS SERVANT.`

segments.voice: Jesus answers at once: I will come and heal him. The officer stops him. In the Douay-Rheims: "Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof: but only say the word, and my servant shall be healed." Then he explains, like a soldier: I'm a man under authority myself, with soldiers under me. I say to one, go, and he goes. To another, come, and he comes. He knows how a word works when it comes from someone with authority. You don't have to walk across town. Just say it. Matthew says Jesus marveled. The one who usually amazes the crowds is amazed himself. He turns to the crowd following him: "Amen I say to you, I have not found so great faith in Israel." A foreigner, an officer of a foreign power, held up as the example. Then Jesus tells him: go, and as you have believed, so be it done to you. The servant is healed in that same hour. Now the Mass. Long ago, in Latin, the Mass borrowed this man's words for the moment before Communion, changing only one thing: instead of my servant, my soul. Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word, and my soul shall be healed. The roof is now the person. A soldier's humble sentence has become the whole Church's.

segments.voice: Let the soldier's sentence move through you slowly, I am not worthy, but only say the word, and hold both halves together for a few breaths: the first is honest, the second trusts. If you go to Mass, listen next time for the whole room saying it at once. If you pray, you can say it now, quietly, for yourself or for someone you're worried about; if not, just let it sit.

40.title: The hem of his cloak (Mark 5:25–34)
40.hook: twelve years bleeding, she reaches through the crowd and Jesus stops to find her
40.howItsDone: Catholics hear this Gospel at Sunday Mass together with the raising of Jairus's daughter, and some bring long illnesses to prayer and to the anointing of the sick.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a centurion said I am not worthy, but only say the word, and the Mass still says it.

A crowd, pushing and shoving down a narrow street. Jesus is on an urgent errand: a synagogue leader's daughter is dying, and you'll hear about her tomorrow. Everyone presses close. And somewhere in that crush is a woman nobody is looking at. For twelve years she's been bleeding. Mark says she had suffered many things from many physicians, spent everything she had, and was no better, but rather worse. Twelve years of appointments, of hope, of bills. She doesn't ask for anything. She doesn't want to be seen. She has one plan, and it's very small.
screen: `A CROWD ON AN URGENT ERRAND.` → `TWELVE YEARS BLEEDING.` → `ONE VERY SMALL PLAN.`

segments.voice: Her plan, in the Douay-Rheims: "If I shall touch but his garment, I shall be whole." She comes up behind him in the crowd and touches his clothes. Matthew and Luke say the hem, the fringe; some readers take that as one of the tassels the Law of Moses asks for at the corners of a garment. At once, Mark says, the bleeding stops, and she feels in her body that she is healed. She could slip away now. Nobody would know. But Jesus stops, turns around in the crowd, and asks: "Who hath touched my garments?" His disciples are baffled: look at this crowd pressing on you, and you ask who touched you? He keeps looking around to see who did it. There's a difference between being bumped and being reached for, and he felt the reach. The woman, afraid and trembling, comes forward, falls down before him, and tells him the whole truth, in front of everyone. Why did he stop? Not to take the healing back. He wanted to meet her. Leviticus counts a flow of blood like hers as ritual impurity, a matter of the Temple, not of sin. Mark doesn't say how her neighbors treated her; he says she'd lost her money and her health. Now, in front of the whole crowd, Jesus calls her by a family word: "Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole: go in peace." Healed in body, then named as family. An old tradition gives her a name, but the Gospels don't.

segments.voice: Think of help you've needed for a long time and haven't asked for: a doctor's appointment you keep postponing, a friend you haven't told, a counselor, a priest, a parent. Maybe you've hoped to get it without anyone seeing; just name it, and imagine reaching out a little, the way she reached for the hem. If you pray, you can reach for God with it.

41.title: Little girl, arise (Mark 5:21–43)
41.hook: a father begs for his daughter, the news comes that she's dead, Jesus goes in anyway
41.howItsDone: Catholics hear the raising of Jairus's daughter at Sunday Mass, and many parents pray for their children by name each day; the story is also read as a sign of hope in the resurrection.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a woman reached for the tassel, and he stopped for her. Now, back to his errand.

His name is Jairus. He's a leader of the synagogue, a respected man, the kind people come to for help. Today he's on his knees in the road. His little daughter is dying. She's twelve. He begs Jesus: come, lay your hands on her, so she'll be healed and live. Jesus goes with him. The crowd, the woman, the stopping, and every minute of that delay is a minute Jairus is counting. While Jesus is still speaking to the woman, men come from Jairus's house. You can see their faces before they say it. Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the teacher any further?
screen: `A FATHER ON HIS KNEES.` → `A DELAY IN THE ROAD.` → `YOUR DAUGHTER IS DEAD.`

segments.voice: Mark says Jesus overheard, and turns to the father before the words can settle. In the Douay-Rheims: "Fear not, only believe." Four words, to a man who has just heard the worst news of his life. Jesus takes only Peter, James and John, and goes to the house. It's full of mourners, weeping and wailing loudly, as people did. He says: why all this noise and weeping? The girl is not dead, but sleeping. They laugh at him. They know dead when they see it. He sends them all out and takes the parents and his three friends in to the girl. He takes her by the hand and speaks to her in Aramaic, the everyday language of home, and Mark keeps the words: "Talitha cumi, which is, being interpreted: Damsel (I say to thee) arise." Talitha: little girl. Cumi: get up. Words a parent might say on an ordinary morning. She gets up and walks around. Mark says they were astonished. Then two tender details. Jesus tells them to give her something to eat. And Mark gives her age, twelve, exactly how long the woman in the crowd had been bleeding. Twelve years of illness, twelve years of life, both brought back on the same afternoon. Some readers think Mark wraps one story inside the other on purpose. Christians read this as one of the stories behind their hope in the resurrection: death spoken to like sleep, and a hand that says get up.

segments.voice: Think of a child you know, a daughter, a son, a niece, a student, the kid next door, and ask what they're carrying right now: fear, sickness, a hard year at school, something you can't fix. If you pray, hold them before God, the way Jairus knelt in the road; if you don't, hold them in your mind with love. Either way, let the two words sit with you: little girl, get up.

42.title: The storm (Mark 4:35–41)
42.hook: he sleeps in the boat, they wake him, he says to the sea peace, be still
42.howItsDone: Catholics hear the calming of the storm at Sunday Mass, and the image of the Church as a boat runs through Catholic art and preaching; the nave of a church takes its name from the Latin for ship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a little girl got up, and the line was fear not, only believe. The week ends on the water, in the dark.

Evening on the Lake of Galilee. After a long day of teaching, Jesus says: let us pass over to the other side. They push off. Some of these men have fished this lake their whole lives. Then the wind comes. The lake sits low, ringed by hills, and storms can drop onto it suddenly and hard. Waves break over the side. The boat is filling. Experienced fishermen are bailing and shouting. And Jesus? Mark says he was in the back of the boat, asleep on a cushion. Asleep. Everything is going under, and the one person who could help doesn't seem to care.
screen: `LET US PASS OVER.` → `A SUDDEN STORM.` → `ASLEEP ON A CUSHION.`

segments.voice: They wake him, and what they say is honest, and a little angry. In the Douay-Rheims: "Master, doth it not concern thee that we perish?" Don't you care? It's one of the most human prayers in the Bible. Jesus gets up, rebukes the wind, and says to the sea: "Peace, be still." In Greek it's two short commands, the words you'd use to quiet a barking dog or a shouting man: be silent, be muzzled. He talks to the storm as if it's a creature that has to obey. The wind drops, and there's a great calm. Then he turns to them: why are you fearful? Have you not faith yet? Here's the twist. Before the storm, they were afraid of the weather. After the calm, Mark says, they feared exceedingly, and said to each other: who is this, that both wind and sea obey him? The calm scares them more than the storm did. The Church has always seen itself in this boat. The main part of a church building is called the nave, from the Latin navis, a ship: the Church is the boat on the water, full of frightened people, with Christ aboard. He doesn't promise there'll be no storms. He's in the boat when it comes. This week has been full of people who reached him in trouble: friends on a roof, a tax collector, a woman at a well, a soldier, a woman in a crowd, a father. Today it's his own friends, bailing water, shouting: don't you care?
screen: `DON'T YOU CARE THAT WE PERISH?` · `BE SILENT, BE MUZZLED.` · `WHO IS THIS?` · `THE NAVE — THE CHURCH AS A BOAT.` · then, large: `PEACE, BE STILL.`

segments.voice: Let one worry come, the one that's been sloshing around all week; don't bail, just notice the waves. Breathe in for four and out for six, and on each out-breath let the words come silently, peace, be still, not ordering the worry away, just letting it quiet a little. If you pray, you can wake him, like they did, with your honest question.
The storm. A boat filling with water, a teacher asleep, and three words to the sea. Today's word.
Your line: peace, be still. Next week: the stories he told, starting with a sower. That's week six.
